\sqrt{100}=10
$$

$$
|p-q|=10
$$

as claimed. If in addition record (4) holds, then

$$
p+q=\frac{4}{15}\cdot pq
$$

$$
\frac{4}{15}\cdot 75=\frac{4\cdot 75}{15}
$$

$$
4\cdot 75=300
$$

$$
\frac{300}{15}=20
$$

$$
p+q=20
$$

Inner piece of the cube identity:

$$
250-75=175
$$

$$
p^{3}+q^{3}=20\cdot 175
$$

$$
20\cdot 100=2000
$$

$$
20\cdot 75=1500
$$

$$
2000+1500=3500
$$

$$
p^{3}+q^{3}=3500
$$

which is exactly the displayed identity.

So the statement is True.

math.title: Mixed Financial Planning: Annuity Due, Continuous Compounding & Growing Perpetuity
math.context: A logistics firm is juggling three separate arrangements. First, a depot lease requires payments of USD 5500 at the BEGINNING of each year as an annuity due for 6 years at 7% interest. Second, the firm separately invests USD 25000 today for 8 years under continuous compounding at a nominal rate of 5.5%. Third, a maintenance reserve is funded as a growing perpetuity that pays USD 2400 at the end of year 1 and then grows at 2% per year forever, discounted at 7%. Decide whether each statement is true or false.
statements: The present value of the annuity-due lease payments is approximately USD 28050.
The future value of these 6 annuity-due payments, evaluated at the end of year 6, is approximately USD 50000.
The USD 25000 investment under continuous compounding at a nominal 5.5% rate accumulates, after 8 years, to approximately USD 38820.
The growing-perpetuity reserve requires a present value that is LESS than the present value of the 6-year annuity-due lease payments.
Comparing the accumulated continuous-compounding investment after 8 years to the growing-perpetuity present value, the continuous-compounding result is LARGER.
tactical_explanations:
**B.** → False

Accumulate the same six annuity-due payments to the end of year 6:

$$
FV_{\mathrm{ad}}=5500\cdot\frac{(1.07)^{6}-1}{0.07}\cdot 1.07
$$

From letter A:

$$
(1.07)^{6}=1.500730351849
$$

$$
(1.07)^{6}-1=0.500730351849
$$

$$
\frac{0.500730351849}{0.07}=7.1532907407
$$

$$
\frac{(1.07)^{6}-1}{0.07}\approx 7.15329
$$

Multiply by the payment:

$$
5500\cdot 7.15329=39343.095
$$

Apply the due shift:

$$
39343.095\cdot 1.07=42097.11165
$$

$$
FV_{\mathrm{ad}}\approx 42097
$$

Compare with the claimed USD 50000:

$$
42097\neq 50000
$$

$$
42097\ngtr 50000
$$

About USD 42100 is far from the claimed USD 50000.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Continuous compounding at nominal force $0.055$ for $8$ years multiplies the principal by $e^{0.055\cdot 8}$:

$$
0.055\cdot 8=0.44
$$

$$
FV_{\mathrm{cont}}=25000\,e^{0.44}
$$

Expand the exponential series for a check, or use the known value:

$$
e^{0.44}\approx 1.55270722
$$

$$
25000\cdot 1.55=38750
$$

$$
25000\cdot 0.00270722=67.6805
$$

$$
38750+67.6805=38817.6805
$$

$$
FV_{\mathrm{cont}}\approx 38818
$$

which matches the claimed USD 38820 to ordinary exam rounding.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The growing-perpetuity present value uses the Gordon formula with first payment at the end of year 1:

$$
PV_{\mathrm{perp}}=\frac{2400}{0.07-0.02}
$$

Denominator:

$$
0.07-0.02=0.05
$$

$$
\frac{2400}{0.05}=48000
$$

$$
PV_{\mathrm{perp}}=48000
$$

From letter A, the annuity-due lease PV is about

$$
PV_{\mathrm{ad}}\approx 28051
$$

Compare:

$$
48000-28051=19949
$$

$$
48000>28051
$$

The perpetuity reserve is larger than the lease PV, not less. The claim that the perpetuity PV is less than the lease PV fails.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Compare the two solved figures from letters C and D side by side.

From the continuous-compounding investment:

$$
0.055\cdot 8=0.44
$$

$$
e^{0.44}\approx 1.55270722
$$

$$
25000\cdot 1.55270722
$$

$$
25000\cdot 1.55=38750
$$

$$
25000\cdot 0.00270722=67.6805
$$

$$
38750+67.6805=38817.6805
$$

$$
FV_{\mathrm{cont}}\approx 38818
$$

From the growing perpetuity:

$$
0.07-0.02=0.05
$$

$$
\frac{2400}{0.05}=48000
$$

$$
PV_{\mathrm{perp}}=48000
$$

Difference:

$$
48000-38818=9182
$$

Check the claimed direction “continuous-compounding result is LARGER”:

$$
38818\ngtr 48000
$$

is false, because

$$
38818<48000
$$

The continuous-compounding accumulation is smaller than the perpetuity PV by about USD 9182, not larger.

So the statement is False.
math.solution_overview:
Three separate cash-flow models share the same 7% discrete rate for the lease and the perpetuity, while the second project compounds continuously.

**Part 1: Setup.**

Annuity-due lease: payment $a=5500$, $n=6$, $r=0.07$, payments at the beginning of each year.

Continuous investment: principal $K=25000$, force $\delta=0.055$, horizon $T=8$.

Growing perpetuity: first end-of-year payment $C=2400$, growth $g=0.02$, discount $r=0.07$.

**Part 2: Power and annuity factors.**

Build $(1.07)^{6}$ by successive multiplication:

$$
1.07^{1}=1.07
$$

$$
1.07^{2}=1.07\cdot 1.07=1.1449
$$

$$
1.07^{3}=1.1449\cdot 1.07=1.225043
$$

$$
1.07^{4}=1.225043\cdot 1.07=1.31079601
$$

$$
1.07^{5}=1.31079601\cdot 1.07=1.4025517307
$$

$$
1.07^{6}=1.4025517307\cdot 1.07=1.500730351849
$$

Ordinary annuity PV factor:

$$
(1.07)^{-6}=\frac{1}{1.500730351849}\approx 0.66634222
$$

$$
1-(1.07)^{-6}\approx 0.33365778
$$

$$
\frac{1-(1.07)^{-6}}{0.07}\approx 4.76653966
$$

Ordinary annuity FV factor:

$$
(1.07)^{6}-1\approx 0.50073035
$$

$$
\frac{(1.07)^{6}-1}{0.07}\approx 7.15329074
$$

**Part 3: Three project values.**

Annuity-due present value (shift one period forward):

$$
PV_{\mathrm{ad}}=5500\cdot 4.76653966\cdot 1.07
$$

$$
5500\cdot 4.76653966\approx 26215.96813
$$

$$
26215.96813\cdot 1.07\approx 28051.09
$$

Annuity-due future value at end of year 6:

$$
FV_{\mathrm{ad}}=5500\cdot 7.15329074\cdot 1.07
$$

$$
5500\cdot 7.15329074\approx 39343.09907
$$

$$
39343.09907\cdot 1.07\approx 42097.12
$$

Continuous compounding:

$$
0.055\cdot 8=0.44
$$

$$
e^{0.44}\approx 1.55270722
$$

$$
FV_{\mathrm{cont}}=25000\cdot 1.55270722\approx 38817.68
$$

Growing perpetuity:

$$
0.07-0.02=0.05
$$

$$
PV_{\mathrm{perp}}=\frac{2400}{0.05}=48000
$$

math.title: Five mixed hard equations — no shortcuts
math.context: Decide whether each claim is true or false. Five independent mixed equations. The five claims deliberately use different judgment styles — candidate survival, root count, size comparison, threshold, and sign/location — so do not expect the same wording twice.
statements: Squaring twice for $\sqrt{3x+7}+\sqrt{x+1}=4$ produces two real candidates, and both of them survive domain checks and back-substitution.
After discarding the poles $x=1$ and $x=-4$, the equation $\dfrac{x+2}{x-1}+\dfrac{2x-3}{x+4}=\dfrac{3x^{2}+5x-2}{(x-1)(x+4)}$ reduces to a linear condition with exactly one surviving real root.
Every real solution of $|x^{2}-6x+5|=3x-4$ is strictly larger than $3$.
Every domain-legal real solution of $\log_{2}(x-1)+\log_{2}(x+3)=\log_{2}(3x+5)$ is strictly larger than $4$.
The equation $\sqrt{x+3}+|x-1|=4$ has at least one negative real solution and at least one real solution greater than $2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Begin with the domain of both radicals. Require

$$
3x+7\ge 0
$$

$$
x\ge -\frac{7}{3}
$$

and

$$
x+1\ge 0
$$

$$
x\ge -1
$$

The intersection is

$$
x\ge -1
$$

Isolate one square root and keep the right-hand side nonnegative:

$$
\sqrt{3x+7}=4-\sqrt{x+1}
$$

$$
4-\sqrt{x+1}\ge 0
$$

$$
\sqrt{x+1}\le 4
$$

$$
x+1\le 16
$$

$$
x\le 15
$$

Square once:

$$
3x+7=\bigl(4-\sqrt{x+1}\bigr)^{2}
$$

$$
3x+7=16-8\sqrt{x+1}+(x+1)
$$

$$
3x+7=17+x-8\sqrt{x+1}
$$

Bring non-radical terms to the left:

$$
3x+7-17-x=-8\sqrt{x+1}
$$

$$
2x-10=-8\sqrt{x+1}
$$

Divide by $-2$:

$$
-(x-5)=4\sqrt{x+1}
$$

$$
5-x=4\sqrt{x+1}
$$

which forces the additional restriction

$$
5-x\ge 0
$$

$$
x\le 5
$$

Square again:

$$
(5-x)^{2}=16(x+1)
$$

$$
25-10x+x^{2}=16x+16
$$

$$
x^{2}-10x-16x+25-16=0
$$

$$
x^{2}-26x+9=0
$$

Discriminant:

$$
26^{2}=676
$$

$$
4\cdot 9=36
$$

$$
676-36=640
$$

$$
\sqrt{640}=\sqrt{64\cdot 10}=8\sqrt{10}
$$

$$
x=\frac{26\pm 8\sqrt{10}}{2}
$$

$$
x=13\pm 4\sqrt{10}
$$

Approximate the two candidates:

$$
\sqrt{10}\approx 3.16227766
$$

$$
4\cdot 3.16227766=12.64911064
$$

$$
x_{+}=13+12.64911064=25.64911064
$$

$$
x_{-}=13-12.64911064=0.35088936
$$

Check against the working interval $[-1,5]$:

$$
25.649\notin [-1,5]
$$

so discard $x_{+}$. The smaller candidate lies in the interval. Back-substitute $x_{-}$:

$$
\sqrt{3\cdot 0.35088936+7}+\sqrt{0.35088936+1}
$$

$$
\sqrt{8.052668}+\sqrt{1.350889}
$$

$$
\approx 2.8377+1.1623=4.0000
$$

which matches. Two real candidates appear, but only one survives. The claim that both survive is false.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Work on the common domain that excludes the poles

$$
x\neq 1
$$

$$
x\neq -4
$$

Clear the common denominator $(x-1)(x+4)$:

$$
(x+2)(x+4)+(2x-3)(x-1)=3x^{2}+5x-2
$$

Expand the first product:

$$
(x+2)(x+4)=x^{2}+4x+2x+8
$$

$$
x^{2}+6x+8
$$

Expand the second product:

$$
(2x-3)(x-1)=2x\cdot x+2x\cdot(-1)+(-3)\cdot x+(-3)\cdot(-1)
$$

$$
2x^{2}-2x-3x+3
$$

$$
2x^{2}-5x+3
$$

Add the left-hand pieces:

$$
x^{2}+6x+8+2x^{2}-5x+3
$$

$$
3x^{2}+(6-5)x+(8+3)
$$

$$
3x^{2}+x+11
$$

Equate to the right-hand side:

$$
3x^{2}+x+11=3x^{2}+5x-2
$$

Subtract $3x^{2}$ from both sides:

$$
x+11=5x-2
$$

Collect $x$-terms:

$$
11+2=5x-x
$$

$$
13=4x
$$

$$
4x=13
$$

$$
x=\frac{13}{4}
$$

$$
\frac{13}{4}=3.25
$$

Check poles:

$$
3.25\neq 1
$$

$$
3.25\neq -4
$$

Exactly one root survives.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

An absolute value equals a real expression only when that expression is nonnegative:

$$
3x-4\ge 0
$$

$$
3x\ge 4
$$

$$
x\ge\frac{4}{3}
$$

The quadratic inside the absolute value factors as

$$
x^{2}-6x+5=(x-1)(x-5)
$$

Case $+$: on the region where $(x-1)(x-5)\ge 0$ and $x\ge\tfrac{4}{3}$,

$$
x^{2}-6x+5=3x-4
$$

$$
x^{2}-9x+9=0
$$

Discriminant:

$$
81-36=45
$$

$$
\sqrt{45}=3\sqrt{5}
$$

$$
x=\frac{9\pm 3\sqrt{5}}{2}
$$

$$
\sqrt{5}\approx 2.23606798
$$

$$
3\cdot 2.23606798=6.70820393
$$

$$
x_{+}=\frac{9+6.70820393}{2}=\frac{15.70820393}{2}=7.85410197
$$

$$
x_{-}=\frac{9-6.70820393}{2}=\frac{2.29179607}{2}=1.14589803
$$

Only $x_{+}\approx 7.85$ lies in the $+$ region with $x\ge\tfrac{4}{3}$ (since $x_{+}>5$). The smaller plus-candidate $1.1459$ fails $x\ge\tfrac{4}{3}\approx 1.333$.

Case $-$: on $(1,5)$ where the quadratic is negative,

$$
-(x^{2}-6x+5)=3x-4
$$

$$
-x^{2}+6x-5=3x-4
$$

$$
-x^{2}+3x-1=0
$$

$$
x^{2}-3x+1=0
$$

$$
x=\frac{3\pm\sqrt{5}}{2}
$$

$$
x=\frac{3+2.23606798}{2}=\frac{5.23606798}{2}=2.61803399
$$

$$
x=\frac{3-2.23606798}{2}=\frac{0.76393202}{2}=0.38196601
$$

Only $x\approx 2.62$ lies in $(1,5)$ and satisfies $x\ge\tfrac{4}{3}$. The surviving roots are therefore approximately $7.85$ and $2.62$. The second root is real and domain-legal, yet

$$
2.62<3
$$

so it is not true that every real solution is strictly larger than $3$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Logarithms force a strict domain. Each argument must be positive:

$$
x-1>0\implies x>1
$$

$$
x+3>0\implies x>-3
$$

$$
3x+5>0\implies x>-\frac{5}{3}
$$

The binding restriction is

$$
x>1
$$

Combine the logs into a single product identity:

$$
\log_{2}(x-1)+\log_{2}(x+3)=\log_{2}\bigl((x-1)(x+3)\bigr)
$$

$$
(x-1)(x+3)=3x+5
$$

Expand the left:

$$
x^{2}+3x-x-3=3x+5
$$

$$
x^{2}+2x-3=3x+5
$$

$$
x^{2}+2x-3-3x-5=0
$$

$$
x^{2}-x-8=0
$$

Discriminant:

$$
1+32=33
$$

$$
x=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{33}}{2}
$$

$$
\sqrt{33}\approx 5.74456265
$$

Plus branch:

$$
\frac{1+5.74456265}{2}=\frac{6.74456265}{2}=3.37228132
$$

Minus branch:

$$
\frac{1-5.74456265}{2}=\frac{-4.74456265}{2}=-2.37228132
$$

Only the plus branch is domain-legal ($x>1$):

$$
\frac{1+\sqrt{33}}{2}\approx 3.37
$$

$$
3.37<4
$$

The unique domain-legal solution is therefore not larger than $4$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Split the absolute value at the kink $x=1$. Domain of the radical requires

$$
x+3\ge 0
$$

$$
x\ge -3
$$

**Right piece** $x\ge 1$: the equation becomes

$$
\sqrt{x+3}+(x-1)=4
$$

$$
\sqrt{x+3}=5-x
$$

Nonnegativity of the right-hand side forces

$$
5-x\ge 0
$$

$$
x\le 5
$$

Square:

$$
x+3=(5-x)^{2}
$$

$$
x+3=25-10x+x^{2}
$$

$$
0=x^{2}-11x+22
$$

$$
x^{2}-11x+22=0
$$

Discriminant:

$$
121-88=33
$$

$$
x=\frac{11\pm\sqrt{33}}{2}
$$

$$
x_{+}=\frac{11+5.74456265}{2}=8.37228132
$$

$$
x_{-}=\frac{11-5.74456265}{2}=2.62771868
$$

Discard $x_{+}$ because $8.37>5$. Keep

$$
x=\frac{11-\sqrt{33}}{2}\approx 2.63>2
$$

Back-check: $\sqrt{2.63+3}+|2.63-1|\approx\sqrt{5.63}+1.63\approx 2.37+1.63=4$. Valid.

**Left piece** $-3\le x<1$:

$$
\sqrt{x+3}+(1-x)=4
$$

$$
\sqrt{x+3}=3+x
$$

Require $3+x\ge 0$, i.e. $x\ge -3$, already in the domain. Square:

$$
x+3=(3+x)^{2}
$$

$$
x+3=9+6x+x^{2}
$$

$$
0=x^{2}+5x+6
$$

$$
x^{2}+5x+6=0
$$

$$
(x+2)(x+3)=0
$$

$$
x=-2\quad\text{or}\quad x=-3
$$

Both are in $[-3,1)$ and both are negative. Back-check $x=-2$:

$$
\sqrt{1}+|-2-1|=1+3=4
$$

Back-check $x=-3$:

$$
\sqrt{0}+|-3-1|=0+4=4
$$

Both valid. So there is at least one negative solution and at least one solution greater than $2$.

So the statement is True.
math.solution_overview:
Five independent mixed equations. Work each letter from its own domain restrictions; none of the five collapses by a one-line sum/product identity.

**Part 1: Radical equation $\sqrt{3x+7}+\sqrt{x+1}=4$.**

Domain of both radicals:

$$
3x+7\ge 0\implies x\ge -\frac{7}{3}
$$

$$
x+1\ge 0\implies x\ge -1
$$

so overall $x\ge -1$. Isolate and keep the right-hand side nonnegative:

$$
\sqrt{3x+7}=4-\sqrt{x+1}
$$

$$
4-\sqrt{x+1}\ge 0\implies x\le 15
$$

Square once, rearrange, and square again to reach

$$
(5-x)^{2}=16(x+1)
$$

$$
x^{2}-26x+9=0
$$

$$
x=13\pm 4\sqrt{10}
$$

Only the smaller root lies in $[-1,5]$ and survives back-substitution.

**Part 2: Rational identity.**

Clear the common denominator $(x-1)(x+4)$ (poles excluded). After expansion the quadratic terms cancel and the linear condition

$$
x+11=5x-2
$$

$$
4x=13
$$

$$
x=\frac{13}{4}
$$

survives.

**Part 3: Absolute value, logs, and mixed radical.**

Absolute-value cases under $x\ge\tfrac{4}{3}$ produce survivors near $7.85$ and $2.62$; logs on $x>1$ yield the unique survivor $(1+\sqrt{33})/2\approx 3.37$; splitting $\sqrt{x+3}+|x-1|=4$ at $x=1$ produces negative roots and a root larger than $2$.

math.title: Print-shop mix — two unknowns, five traps
math.context:
A print shop sells only mono pages and colour pages. In one batch it printed a total of $180$ pages and booked revenue EUR 8100. Mono sells at EUR 35 each and colour at EUR 55 each:
$$
m+c=180,\qquad 35m+55c=8100.
$$
The unique baseline solution is the factual starting point. Decide whether each statement is true or false.
statements: The unique baseline solution is $(m,c)=(90,90)$.
If the colour price had been EUR 60 instead of EUR 55, with the same count $m+c=180$ and the same revenue EUR 8100, then $c$ would have fallen below $75$.
If management had printed $15$ fewer mono pages and $15$ more colour pages than the baseline, revenue would have risen by exactly EUR 300.
If total pages stayed $180$ but the revenue target rose to EUR 10000 at the same prices, no nonnegative solution $(m,c)$ would exist, because an all-colour batch only reaches EUR 9900.
If prices stayed EUR 35 and EUR 55 but the shop printed the swapped mix $(120,60)$ instead of the baseline $(90,90)$, revenue would still be EUR 8100.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Eliminate $m$ by substituting $m=180-c$ into the revenue equation:

$$
35(180-c)+55c=8100
$$

First the constant piece:

$$
35\cdot 180
$$

$$
35\cdot 100=3500
$$

$$
35\cdot 80=2800
$$

$$
3500+2800=6300
$$

$$
35\cdot 180=6300
$$

Distribute:

$$
6300-35c+55c=8100
$$

Combine like terms:

$$
(-35+55)c=20c
$$

$$
6300+20c=8100
$$

Isolate the colour term:

$$
20c=8100-6300
$$

$$
8100-6300=1800
$$

$$
20c=1800
$$

$$
c=\frac{1800}{20}
$$

$$
\frac{1800}{20}=90
$$

$$
c=90
$$

$$
m=180-90
$$

$$
180-90=90
$$

$$
m=90
$$

The unique baseline solution is therefore $(m,c)=(90,90)$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Keep the page total $m+c=180$ and the revenue $8100$, but replace the colour price by $60$:

$$
m=180-c
$$

$$
35(180-c)+60c=8100
$$

Compute the constant piece:

$$
35\cdot 180
$$

$$
35\cdot 100=3500
$$

$$
35\cdot 80=2800
$$

$$
3500+2800=6300
$$

Distribute:

$$
6300-35c+60c=8100
$$

Combine the colour coefficients:

$$
-35+60=25
$$

$$
6300+25c=8100
$$

Isolate:

$$
25c=8100-6300
$$

$$
8100-6300=1800
$$

$$
25c=1800
$$

$$
c=\frac{1800}{25}
$$

$$
25\cdot 72=1800
$$

$$
c=72
$$

Also recover mono:

$$
m=180-72=108
$$

Compare the colour count with the claimed threshold:

$$
72<75
$$

the new colour count falls below $75$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

From the baseline $(90,90)$, shift by $15$ pages toward colour:

$$
m=90-15
$$

$$
90-15=75
$$

$$
c=90+15
$$

$$
90+15=105
$$

$$
(m,c)=(75,105)
$$

Revenue at the new mix, product by product. First the mono contribution:

$$
35\cdot 75
$$

$$
35\cdot 70=2450
$$

$$
35\cdot 5=175
$$

$$
2450+175=2625
$$

$$
35\cdot 75=2625
$$

Next the colour contribution:

$$
55\cdot 105
$$

$$
55\cdot 100=5500
$$

$$
55\cdot 5=275
$$

$$
5500+275=5775
$$

$$
55\cdot 105=5775
$$

Add the two pieces:

$$
2625+5775=8400
$$

Revenue rise against the baseline EUR 8100:

$$
8400-8100=300
$$

Revenue rises by exactly EUR 300.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

An all-colour batch of $180$ pages yields the maximum feasible revenue at the given prices. Compute that ceiling:

$$
55\cdot 180
$$

$$
55\cdot 100=5500
$$

$$
55\cdot 80=4400
$$

$$
5500+4400=9900
$$

$$
55\cdot 180=9900
$$

Any mix that includes mono pages earns strictly less, because mono is cheaper than colour:

$$
35<55
$$

Replacing one colour page by one mono page cuts revenue by

$$
55-35=20
$$

euros per swapped page. Therefore every nonnegative mix $(m,c)$ with $m+c=180$ satisfies

$$
35m+55c\le 9900
$$

A target of EUR 10000 exceeds that ceiling:

$$
10000>9900
$$

$$
10000-9900=100
$$

so no nonnegative solution $(m,c)$ exists.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Revenue at the swapped mix $(120,60)$, product by product. First mono:

$$
35\cdot 120
$$

$$
35\cdot 100=3500
$$

$$
35\cdot 20=700
$$

$$
3500+700=4200
$$

$$
35\cdot 120=4200
$$

Then colour:

$$
55\cdot 60
$$

$$
50\cdot 60=3000
$$

$$
5\cdot 60=300
$$

$$
3000+300=3300
$$

$$
55\cdot 60=3300
$$

Sum:

$$
4200+3300=7500
$$

Compare with the baseline revenue EUR 8100:

$$
7500\neq 8100
$$

Difference:

$$
8100-7500=600
$$

Alternatively, relative to baseline $(90,90)$, the swap moves $30$ pages from colour to mono, each costing

$$
55-35=20
$$

euros:

$$
30\cdot 20=600
$$

The swapped mix earns EUR 600 less than EUR 8100, so it does not preserve the baseline revenue.

So the statement is False.

math.title: Hard mixed inequalities — varied interval claims
math.context: Decide whether each claim is true or false. All five letters are inequalities, but the claims are worded differently on purpose: absence of counterexamples, existence inside an open interval, existence on a closed interval, containment of a segment, and nonempty intersection.
statements: No point of the interval $[1,4]$ violates $|x^{2}-5x+4|+|2x-3|\le x+6$.
The inequality $\sqrt{2x+5}+|x-2|\le 4$ admits at least one solution in the open interval $(1,2)$.
There exists some $x\in[0,1]$ for which $\dfrac{x^{2}-5x+6}{x^{2}-x-2}\ge 1$.
The solution set of $\dfrac{|x|}{x+3}+\sqrt{x+1}\le 2$ contains every point of $[0,1]$.
The inequality $\dfrac{|2x-5|}{|x+1|}+|x-2|\le 4$ has nonempty intersection with the interval $[-4,-2]$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The claim is a universal “no counterexample” statement on the closed interval $[1,4]$. Factor the first absolute expression:

$$
x^{2}-5x+4=(x-1)(x-4)
$$

Critical points inside $[1,4]$ are $x=1$, $x=4$, and the kink of $|2x-3|$ at

$$
2x-3=0
$$

$$
x=\frac{3}{2}
$$

**Piece** $[1,\tfrac{3}{2}]$: here $(x-1)(x-4)\le 0$ so $|x^{2}-5x+4|=-(x^{2}-5x+4)$, and $2x-3\le 0$ so $|2x-3|=3-2x$. The inequality becomes

$$
-(x^{2}-5x+4)+(3-2x)\le x+6
$$

$$
-x^{2}+5x-4+3-2x\le x+6
$$

$$
-x^{2}+3x-1\le x+6
$$

Bring all terms to the right:

$$
0\le x^{2}-3x+1+x+6
$$

$$
0\le x^{2}-2x+7
$$

Discriminant of $x^{2}-2x+7$:

$$
(-2)^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 7
$$

$$
4-28=-24
$$

$$
-24<0
$$

and the leading coefficient is positive, so $x^{2}-2x+7>0$ for every real $x$. The inequality holds identically on this piece.

**Piece** $[\tfrac{3}{2},4]$: still $|x^{2}-5x+4|=-(x^{2}-5x+4)$, but now $|2x-3|=2x-3$. The inequality becomes

$$
-(x^{2}-5x+4)+(2x-3)\le x+6
$$

$$
-x^{2}+5x-4+2x-3\le x+6
$$

$$
-x^{2}+7x-7\le x+6
$$

$$
0\le x^{2}-7x+7+x+6
$$

$$
0\le x^{2}-6x+13
$$

Discriminant of $x^{2}-6x+13$:

$$
36-52=-16
$$

$$
-16<0
$$

again always positive. Hence no point of $[1,4]$ is a counterexample.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The claim only asks for existence inside the open interval $(1,2)$. Domain of the radical requires

$$
2x+5\ge 0
$$

$$
x\ge -\frac{5}{2}
$$

which already contains $(1,2)$. Pick the convenient interior test point

$$
x=\frac{3}{2}
$$

Left-hand side:

$$
\sqrt{2\cdot\frac{3}{2}+5}+\left|\frac{3}{2}-2\right|
$$

$$
2\cdot\frac{3}{2}=3
$$

$$
3+5=8
$$

$$
\sqrt{8}=\sqrt{4\cdot 2}=2\sqrt{2}
$$

$$
\sqrt{2}\approx 1.41421356
$$

$$
2\sqrt{2}\approx 2.82842712
$$

$$
\left|\frac{3}{2}-2\right|=\left|-\frac{1}{2}\right|=\frac{1}{2}
$$

$$
2.82842712+0.5=3.32842712
$$

Compare with $4$:

$$
3.32842712\le 4
$$

So at least one point of $(1,2)$ satisfies the inequality.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Ask whether any point of the closed interval $[0,1]$ can satisfy the rational inequality. Factor numerator and denominator:

$$
x^{2}-5x+6=(x-2)(x-3)
$$

$$
x^{2}-x-2=(x-2)(x+1)
$$

Poles are

$$
x=-1
$$

$$
x=2
$$

For every other $x$,

$$
\frac{x^{2}-5x+6}{x^{2}-x-2}-1=\frac{(x-2)(x-3)-(x-2)(x+1)}{(x-2)(x+1)}
$$

Numerator of the difference:

$$
(x-2)\bigl((x-3)-(x+1)\bigr)
$$

$$
(x-3)-(x+1)=x-3-x-1=-4
$$

$$
\frac{(x-2)(-4)}{(x-2)(x+1)}=\frac{-4}{x+1}
$$

so the inequality $\dfrac{x^{2}-5x+6}{x^{2}-x-2}\ge 1$ reduces to

$$
\frac{-4}{x+1}\ge 0
$$

$$
\frac{4}{x+1}\le 0
$$

which holds precisely when

$$
x+1<0
$$

$$
x<-1
$$

The interval $[0,1]$ lies entirely outside that half-line. In particular at $x=0$:

$$
\frac{0-0+6}{0-0-2}=\frac{6}{-2}=-3
$$

$$
-3\ngeq 1
$$

No point of $[0,1]$ works.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The claim asks for containment of the whole segment $[0,1]$ in the solution set. On $[0,1]$ one has $x\ge 0$, so

$$
|x|=x
$$

and both

$$
x+3>0
$$

$$
x+1\ge 0
$$

The inequality reads

$$
\frac{x}{x+3}+\sqrt{x+1}\le 2
$$

Each summand is increasing on $[0,1]$: the derivative of $\dfrac{x}{x+3}$ is $\dfrac{3}{(x+3)^{2}}>0$, and $\sqrt{x+1}$ is increasing. So the left-hand side is maximized at the right endpoint $x=1$:

$$
\frac{1}{1+3}+\sqrt{1+1}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{4}+\sqrt{2}
$$

$$
0.25+\sqrt{2}
$$

$$
\sqrt{2}\approx 1.41421356
$$

$$
0.25+1.41421356=1.66421356
$$

$$
1.66421356\le 2
$$

At the left endpoint $x=0$:

$$
\frac{0}{3}+\sqrt{1}=0+1=1
$$

$$
1\le 2
$$

Because the maximum on the segment is already $\le 2$, every point of $[0,1]$ belongs to the solution set.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The claim asks whether the solution set meets $[-4,-2]$. The pole $x=-1$ does not meet that interval, so every point of $[-4,-2]$ is domain-legal. Test the convenient interior point $x=-3$:

$$
\frac{|2(-3)-5|}{|-3+1|}+|-3-2|
$$

$$
2\cdot(-3)=-6
$$

$$
|-6-5|=|-11|=11
$$

$$
|-3+1|=|-2|=2
$$

$$
\frac{11}{2}=5.5
$$

$$
|-3-2|=|-5|=5
$$

$$
5.5+5=10.5
$$

Compare with $4$:

$$
10.5\le 4
$$

is false:

$$
10.5\ngtr 4?\quad\text{no: }10.5>4
$$

Check the left endpoint $x=-4$:

$$
\frac{|2(-4)-5|}{|-4+1|}+|-4-2|
$$

$$
|-8-5|=13
$$

$$
|-3|=3
$$

$$
\frac{13}{3}\approx 4.333
$$

$$
|-6|=6
$$

$$
4.333+6=10.333>4
$$

Check the right endpoint $x=-2$:

$$
\frac{|2(-2)-5|}{|-2+1|}+|-2-2|
$$

$$
|-4-5|=9
$$

$$
|-1|=1
$$

$$
\frac{9}{1}=9
$$

$$
|-4|=4
$$

$$
9+4=13>4
$$

The expression stays larger than $4$ throughout $[-4,-2]$. The intersection with $[-4,-2]$ is therefore empty.

So the statement is False.
math.solution_overview:
Five mixed inequalities with deliberately varied claim styles: no-counterexample, existence in an open interval, existence on a closed interval, segment containment, and nonempty intersection.

**Part 1: Absolute-value inequality on $[1,4]$.**

Critical points of $|x^{2}-5x+4|+|2x-3|\le x+6$ on $[1,4]$ are $x=1$, $x=\tfrac{3}{2}$, and $x=4$. On $[1,\tfrac{3}{2}]$:

$$
-(x^{2}-5x+4)+(3-2x)\le x+6
$$

$$
-x^{2}+5x-4+3-2x\le x+6
$$

$$
-x^{2}+3x-1\le x+6
$$

$$
0\le x^{2}-2x+7
$$

Discriminant of $x^{2}-2x+7$:

$$
4-28=-24<0
$$

so the quadratic is always positive. On $[\tfrac{3}{2},4]$:

$$
0\le x^{2}-6x+13
$$

$$
36-52=-16<0
$$

again always positive. No counterexample on $[1,4]$.

**Part 2: Existence checks.**

For $\sqrt{2x+5}+|x-2|\le 4$, domain $x\ge -\tfrac{5}{2}$. Interior test at $x=\tfrac{3}{2}\in(1,2)$:

$$
\sqrt{8}+\tfrac{1}{2}=2\sqrt{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}\approx 3.328\le 4
$$

witnesses existence.

For the rational inequality, cancel $x-2$ away from the poles to obtain $-4/(x+1)\ge 0$, i.e. $x<-1$; the segment $[0,1]$ lies entirely outside that half-line.

**Part 3: Containment and empty intersection.**

On $[0,1]$ the left-hand side of $\dfrac{|x|}{x+3}+\sqrt{x+1}\le 2$ is increasing and its maximum at $x=1$ is still $\le 2$. On $[-4,-2]$ the expression $\dfrac{|2x-5|}{|x+1|}+|x-2|$ stays larger than $4$ (e.g. $10.5$ at $x=-3$).

math.title: Parametric quadratic family — critical cases
math.context:
For each real parameter $k$, define
$$
g_k(x)=x^{2}-(2k+1)x+(k^{2}-4).
$$
Decide whether each claim about this family is true or false.
statements: For every real $k$, the equation $g_k(x)=0$ has two distinct real roots.
The axis of symmetry of $y=g_k(x)$ is $x=k+\tfrac12$ for every $k$.
If $k=2$, then the roots are $x=1$ and $x=5$.
There exists a real $k$ for which both roots are equal to $0$.
The vertex $y$-coordinate equals $-\dfrac{17}{4}$ when $k=0$.
math.solution_overview:
A one-parameter quadratic family. Read the axis, discriminant, and vertex from the coefficients; then specialise $k$ only when a letter asks for it.

**Part 1: Setup.**

$$
g_k(x)=x^{2}-(2k+1)x+(k^{2}-4)
$$

Write the standard coefficients:

$$
a=1
$$

$$
B=2k+1
$$

$$
C=k^{2}-4
$$

**Part 2: Axis and discriminant.**

Axis of symmetry:

$$
x=\frac{B}{2a}=\frac{2k+1}{2}
$$

$$
\frac{2k+1}{2}=k+\frac{1}{2}
$$

Discriminant expansion:

$$
\Delta=(2k+1)^{2}-4(k^{2}-4)
$$

$$
(2k+1)^{2}=4k^{2}+4k+1
$$

$$
4(k^{2}-4)=4k^{2}-16
$$

$$
\Delta=4k^{2}+4k+1-(4k^{2}-16)
$$

$$
\Delta=4k^{2}+4k+1-4k^{2}+16
$$

$$
\Delta=4k+17
$$

**Part 3: Vertex $y$-value and special cases.**

For a monic quadratic the vertex height is $-\Delta/4$:

$$
g_k\Bigl(k+\tfrac12\Bigr)=-\frac{\Delta}{4}=-\frac{4k+17}{4}
$$

At $k=0$:

$$
\Delta=17
$$

$$
-\frac{17}{4}
$$

At $k=2$:

$$
g_2(x)=x^{2}-5x=x(x-5)
$$

roots $0$ and $5$. A double root at $0$ would need both $C=0$ and $B=0$, which force incompatible values of $k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Two distinct real roots require a strictly positive discriminant. Expand

$$
\Delta=(2k+1)^{2}-4(k^{2}-4)
$$

First square:

$$
(2k+1)^{2}=4k^{2}+4k+1
$$

Then the second term:

$$
4(k^{2}-4)=4k^{2}-16
$$

Subtract:

$$
\Delta=4k^{2}+4k+1-(4k^{2}-16)
$$

$$
\Delta=4k^{2}+4k+1-4k^{2}+16
$$

$$
\Delta=4k+17
$$

At $k=-5$:

$$
\Delta=4(-5)+17
$$

$$
4\cdot(-5)=-20
$$

$$
-20+17=-3
$$

$$
\Delta=-3<0
$$

so $g_{-5}$ has no real roots. The claim that every real $k$ yields two distinct real roots fails.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

For a monic quadratic written as

$$
x^{2}-Bx+C
$$

the axis of symmetry is the vertical line

$$
x=\frac{B}{2}
$$

Here the linear coefficient is

$$
B=2k+1
$$

so

$$
x=\frac{2k+1}{2}
$$

Split the fraction into two pieces:

$$
\frac{2k+1}{2}=\frac{2k}{2}+\frac{1}{2}
$$

$$
\frac{2k}{2}=k
$$

$$
x=k+\frac{1}{2}
$$

This identity holds for every real parameter $k$; no discriminant restriction appears. As a quick check at $k=0$:

$$
x=0+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}
$$

and at $k=2$:

$$
x=2+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{5}{2}
$$

which matches $B=5$ giving axis $x=\tfrac{5}{2}$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Substitute $k=2$ into each coefficient carefully.

Linear coefficient:

$$
2k+1=2\cdot 2+1
$$

$$
2\cdot 2=4
$$

$$
4+1=5
$$

Constant term:

$$
k^{2}-4
$$

$$
2^{2}=4
$$

$$
4-4=0
$$

The specialised quadratic is therefore

$$
g_2(x)=x^{2}-5x+0
$$

$$
g_2(x)=x^{2}-5x
$$

Factor out the common $x$:

$$
g_2(x)=x(x-5)
$$

Set equal to zero:

$$
x=0
$$

or

$$
x-5=0
$$

$$
x=5
$$

The two roots are $0$ and $5$. The claim asserts the roots are $1$ and $5$. Compare:

$$
0\neq 1
$$

$$
5=5
$$

Only one of the two claimed roots is correct, so the statement as a whole is false.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

A double root at $0$ would require both $g_k(0)=0$ and $g_k'(0)=0$. First the constant term:

$$
g_k(0)=k^{2}-4
$$

$$
k^{2}-4=0
$$

$$
k^{2}=4
$$

$$
k=2\quad\text{or}\quad k=-2
$$

Differentiate:

$$
g_k'(x)=2x-(2k+1)
$$

$$
g_k'(0)=-(2k+1)
$$

Set the derivative condition:

$$
-(2k+1)=0
$$

$$
2k+1=0
$$

$$
2k=-1
$$

$$
k=-\frac{1}{2}
$$

Check whether $k=-\tfrac12$ satisfies $k^{2}-4=0$:

$$
\Bigl(-\frac{1}{2}\Bigr)^{2}=\frac{1}{4}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{4}-4=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{16}{4}=-\frac{15}{4}
$$

$$
-\frac{15}{4}\neq 0
$$

Conversely, at $k=2$:

$$
g_2'(0)=-(4+1)=-5\neq 0
$$

At $k=-2$:

$$
g_{-2}'(0)=-(-4+1)=-(-3)=3\neq 0
$$

The two conditions are incompatible, so no such $k$ exists.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

For $k=0$ the quadratic is

$$
g_0(x)=x^{2}-(0+1)x+(0-4)
$$

$$
g_0(x)=x^{2}-x-4
$$

The axis from letter B is

$$
x=0+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}
$$

Evaluate:

$$
g_0\Bigl(\frac{1}{2}\Bigr)=\Bigl(\frac{1}{2}\Bigr)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}-4
$$

$$
\Bigl(\frac{1}{2}\Bigr)^{2}=\frac{1}{4}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{2}{4}=-\frac{1}{4}
$$

$$
-\frac{1}{4}-4=-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{16}{4}=-\frac{17}{4}
$$

$$
g_0\Bigl(\frac{1}{2}\Bigr)=-\frac{17}{4}
$$

Alternatively via the discriminant shortcut:

$$
\Delta=4\cdot 0+17=17
$$

$$
-\frac{\Delta}{4}=-\frac{17}{4}
$$

which matches the claimed vertex $y$-coordinate.

So the statement is True.

math.title: Courier tariff — affine day/night word problem
math.context: A courier charges a daytime base fee of EUR 12 plus EUR 0.8 per kilometre. Night runs use the same kilometre rate but add a flat night surcharge of EUR 5. Let $d>0$ be the distance in kilometres. Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: The daytime bill for distance $d$ is exactly $12+0.8d$ euros.
If the same distance were run at night, the night bill would be exactly EUR 5 more than the daytime bill for every $d>0$.
There is a distance $d^{*}$ at which a daytime run and a night run would cost the same; solving $12+0.8d=12+0.8d+5$ finds it.
If the firm waived the EUR 12 base on daytime runs only (charging pure $0.8d$), then for a $20$ km daytime job the client would save exactly EUR 12 compared with the original daytime tariff.
If distance doubled from $10$ km to $20$ km on a daytime run, the bill would also double, because both the base and the kilometre charge scale linearly with $d$.
math.solution_overview:
Day and night courier tariffs are affine in distance $d>0$. Night keeps the same kilometre rate and adds a flat surcharge, so the two cost graphs are parallel vertical translates.

**Part 1: Setup — the two tariffs.**

Daytime base fee (euros):

$$
12
$$

Daytime kilometre rate (euros per km):

$$
0.8
$$

Night flat surcharge (euros):

$$
5
$$

Daytime cost:

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)=12+0.8d
$$

Night cost starts from the day formula and adds the surcharge:

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)=12+0.8d+5
$$

$$
12+5=17
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)=17+0.8d
$$

Same slope on both:

$$
\frac{d}{dd}C_{\mathrm{day}}=0.8
$$

$$
\frac{d}{dd}C_{\mathrm{night}}=0.8
$$

Constant vertical gap:

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)-C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)=5
$$

**Part 2: Shared numerical evaluations.**

Kilometre charge at $d=5$:

$$
0.8\times 5=4
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(5)=12+4=16
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(5)=17+4=21
$$

Kilometre charge at $d=10$:

$$
0.8\times 10=8
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(10)=12+8=20
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(10)=17+8=25
$$

Kilometre charge at $d=20$:

$$
0.8\times 20=16
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(20)=12+16=28
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(20)=17+16=33
$$

Waived-base daytime charge at $d=20$:

$$
0.8\times 20=16
$$

Saving versus original daytime bill:

$$
28-16=12
$$

**Part 3: Break-even and doubling checks.**

Set day equal to night:

$$
12+0.8d=12+0.8d+5
$$

$$
0=5
$$

Contradiction, so no break-even $d^{*}$. Doubling $10\to 20$:

$$
\frac{C_{\mathrm{day}}(20)}{C_{\mathrm{day}}(10)}=\frac{28}{20}=1.4
$$

$$
1.4\neq 2
$$

so the bill does not double with distance.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Read the daytime tariff from the stem: a fixed base of EUR $12$ plus EUR $0.8$ per kilometre. Write the base alone:

$$
12
$$

Write the per-kilometre rate alone:

$$
0.8
$$

Write the kilometre charge as a product with distance:

$$
0.8\cdot d
$$

Add base and kilometre charge:

$$
12+0.8d
$$

So the daytime bill is

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)=12+0.8d
$$

Spot-check at $d=10$:

$$
0.8\times 10=8
$$

$$
12+8=20
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(10)=20
$$

Spot-check at $d=20$:

$$
0.8\times 20
$$

$$
0.8\times 10=8
$$

$$
8+8=16
$$

$$
0.8\times 20=16
$$

$$
12+16=28
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(20)=28
$$

Spot-check at $d=5$:

$$
0.8\times 5=4
$$

$$
12+4=16
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(5)=16
$$

Spot-check at $d=25$:

$$
0.8\times 25
$$

$$
0.8\times 20=16
$$

$$
0.8\times 5=4
$$

$$
16+4=20
$$

$$
12+20=32
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(25)=32
$$

Each check equals $12+0.8d$ euros. The claimed daytime formula matches the tariff exactly.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Night runs keep the kilometre rate $0.8$ and add a flat surcharge of EUR $5$. Start from the daytime bill:

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)=12+0.8d
$$

Add the night surcharge as its own step:

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)=C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)+5
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)=12+0.8d+5
$$

Combine the constant terms:

$$
12+5=17
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)=17+0.8d
$$

Form the difference night minus day:

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)-C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)
$$

$$
(17+0.8d)-(12+0.8d)
$$

Constants:

$$
17-12=5
$$

Kilometre terms cancel:

$$
0.8d-0.8d=0
$$

$$
5+0=5
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)-C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)=5
$$

Verify at three distances. At $d=10$:

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(10)=12+0.8\times 10
$$

$$
0.8\times 10=8
$$

$$
12+8=20
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(10)=17+8=25
$$

$$
25-20=5
$$

At $d=20$:

$$
0.8\times 20=16
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(20)=12+16=28
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(20)=17+16=33
$$

$$
33-28=5
$$

At $d=5$:

$$
0.8\times 5=4
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(5)=12+4=16
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(5)=17+4=21
$$

$$
21-16=5
$$

For every $d>0$ the night bill is exactly EUR $5$ more than the daytime bill.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The claim asks for a break-even distance $d^{*}$ by solving

$$
12+0.8d=12+0.8d+5
$$

Subtract $12$ from both sides:

$$
0.8d=0.8d+5
$$

Subtract $0.8d$ from both sides:

$$
0=5
$$

Check whether that identity can hold:

$$
0\neq 5
$$

Equivalently, rewrite the night formula first:

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)=12+0.8d+5
$$

$$
12+5=17
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)=17+0.8d
$$

Set equal to day:

$$
12+0.8d=17+0.8d
$$

Subtract $0.8d$:

$$
12=17
$$

$$
12\neq 17
$$

Or look at the constant gap already computed:

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(d)-C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)=5
$$

$$
5\neq 0
$$

Try a concrete candidate such as $d=10$:

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(10)=12+8=20
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(10)=17+8=25
$$

$$
20\neq 25
$$

Try $d=20$:

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(20)=12+16=28
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{night}}(20)=17+16=33
$$

$$
28\neq 33
$$

Parallel affine tariffs with a positive gap never meet. No real $d^{*}$ exists, and the displayed equation collapses to the absurdity $0=5$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Original daytime bill at $d=20$. First form the kilometre piece by splitting the product:

$$
0.8\times 20
$$

$$
0.8\times 10=8
$$

$$
0.8\times 10=8
$$

$$
8+8=16
$$

$$
0.8\times 20=16
$$

Add the daytime base:

$$
12+16
$$

$$
12+16=28
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(20)=28
$$

Waiving the EUR $12$ base leaves only the kilometre charge:

$$
0.8\times 20=16
$$

Saving versus the original daytime tariff:

$$
28-16
$$

$$
28-10=18
$$

$$
18-6=12
$$

$$
28-16=12
$$

Alternatively, the saving is exactly the waived base fee itself:

$$
12
$$

$$
12=12
$$

Cross-check the arithmetic with a second distance $d=10$ under the same waiver logic (saving still equals the base):

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(10)=12+0.8\times 10
$$

$$
0.8\times 10=8
$$

$$
12+8=20
$$

$$
20-8=12
$$

At every daytime distance the waiver saves exactly EUR $12$, matching the claim for the $20$ km job.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Evaluate the daytime bill at $d=10$. Kilometre piece:

$$
0.8\times 10=8
$$

Add the base:

$$
12+8=20
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(10)=20
$$

Evaluate at $d=20$. Kilometre piece:

$$
0.8\times 20=16
$$

Add the base:

$$
12+16=28
$$

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(20)=28
$$

Form the ratio of the two bills:

$$
\frac{C_{\mathrm{day}}(20)}{C_{\mathrm{day}}(10)}=\frac{28}{20}
$$

$$
\frac{28}{20}=\frac{7}{5}
$$

$$
\frac{7}{5}=1.4
$$

Compare with doubling:

$$
1.4\neq 2
$$

If the bill truly doubled with distance, we would need

$$
2\times C_{\mathrm{day}}(10)
$$

$$
2\times 20=40
$$

but

$$
C_{\mathrm{day}}(20)=28
$$

and

$$
28\neq 40
$$

Separate the base and kilometre pieces. Base at both distances:

$$
12
$$

$$
12
$$

(the base does not scale). Kilometre piece at $10$:

$$
8
$$

Kilometre piece at $20$:

$$
16
$$

$$
\frac{16}{8}=2
$$

Only the kilometre part doubles; the fixed base of EUR $12$ does not. Homogeneity would require $C_{\mathrm{day}}(2d)=2\,C_{\mathrm{day}}(d)$; at $d=10$ that needs $28=40$, which fails.

So the statement is False.

math.title: Cubic over quadratic — limits and roots
math.context:
Let
$$
r(x)=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d,\qquad a\neq 0,
$$
be a real cubic, and define
$$
s(x)=\dfrac{r(x)}{x^{2}+4}.
$$
Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to+\infty}s(x)=+\infty$ whenever $a>0$.
$\displaystyle\lim_{x\to-\infty}r(x)=-\infty$ whenever $a>0$.
If $r(2)=0$ and $r'(2)=0$, then $(x-2)^{2}$ divides $r(x)$, so $x=2$ is at least a double root.
For every choice of $a,b,c,d$ with $a\neq 0$, the horizontal line $y=0$ is a horizontal asymptote of $s$.
If $a=3$, $b=-6$, $c=0$, $d=0$, then $r(x)=3x^{2}(x-2)$, so $x=0$ is a double root and $x=2$ is a simple root.
math.solution_overview:
A real cubic $r$ sits over the always-positive quadratic denominator $x^{2}+4$. Asymptotics of the quotient $s=r/(x^{2}+4)$ follow from degree comparison; multiple roots of $r$ follow from shared zeros with $r'$.

**Part 1: Setup.**

$$
r(x)=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d,\qquad a\neq 0
$$

$$
s(x)=\frac{r(x)}{x^{2}+4}
$$

Degree of the numerator:

$$
\deg r=3
$$

Degree of the denominator:

$$
\deg(x^{2}+4)=2
$$

Compare:

$$
3>2
$$

Derivative of the cubic:

$$
r'(x)=3ax^{2}+2bx+c
$$

**Part 2: Asymptotic rewrite of $s$.**

Factor $ax^{3}$ from the numerator and $x^{2}$ from the denominator:

$$
s(x)=\frac{ax^{3}\bigl(1+\frac{b}{ax}+\frac{c}{ax^{2}}+\frac{d}{ax^{3}}\bigr)}{x^{2}\bigl(1+\frac{4}{x^{2}}\bigr)}
$$

Leading ratio:

$$
\frac{ax^{3}}{x^{2}}=ax
$$

$$
s(x)=ax\cdot\frac{1+\frac{b}{ax}+\frac{c}{ax^{2}}+\frac{d}{ax^{3}}}{1+\frac{4}{x^{2}}}
$$

As $|x|\to\infty$ each of $\frac{b}{ax}$, $\frac{c}{ax^{2}}$, $\frac{d}{ax^{3}}$, $\frac{4}{x^{2}}$ tends to $0$, so the fraction tends to $1$ and

$$
s(x)\sim ax
$$

In particular $|s(x)|\to\infty$, so $y=0$ cannot be a horizontal asymptote.

**Part 3: Multiple roots and the concrete example.**

If $r(2)=0$ and $r'(2)=0$, then $(x-2)^{2}$ divides $r(x)$. For $a=3$, $b=-6$, $c=0$, $d=0$:

$$
r(x)=3x^{3}-6x^{2}
$$

$$
3x^{3}-6x^{2}=3x^{2}(x-2)
$$

Check by expanding:

$$
3x^{2}\cdot x=3x^{3}
$$

$$
3x^{2}\cdot(-2)=-6x^{2}
$$

$$
3x^{3}-6x^{2}=3x^{3}-6x^{2}
$$

so $x=0$ is a double root and $x=2$ is a simple root.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Start from the definition:

$$
s(x)=\frac{ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d}{x^{2}+4}
$$

Factor $ax^{3}$ in the numerator:

$$
ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d=ax^{3}\Bigl(1+\frac{b}{ax}+\frac{c}{ax^{2}}+\frac{d}{ax^{3}}\Bigr)
$$

Factor $x^{2}$ in the denominator:

$$
x^{2}+4=x^{2}\Bigl(1+\frac{4}{x^{2}}\Bigr)
$$

Leading ratio:

$$
\frac{ax^{3}}{x^{2}}=ax
$$

$$
s(x)=ax\cdot\frac{1+\frac{b}{ax}+\frac{c}{ax^{2}}+\frac{d}{ax^{3}}}{1+\frac{4}{x^{2}}}
$$

Send $x\to+\infty$ term by term:

$$
\frac{b}{ax}\to 0
$$

$$
\frac{c}{ax^{2}}\to 0
$$

$$
\frac{d}{ax^{3}}\to 0
$$

$$
\frac{4}{x^{2}}\to 0
$$

so the fraction tends to $1$:

$$
\frac{1+0+0+0}{1+0}=1
$$

$$
s(x)\sim ax
$$

Whenever $a>0$ and $x\to+\infty$:

$$
ax\to+\infty
$$

$$
\lim_{x\to+\infty}s(x)=+\infty
$$

Numerical check with $a=3$, $b=c=d=0$ at a large $x$:

$$
s(100)=\frac{3\cdot 100^{3}}{100^{2}+4}
$$

$$
100^{2}=10000
$$

$$
100^{3}=1000000
$$

$$
3\cdot 1000000=3000000
$$

$$
10000+4=10004
$$

$$
\frac{3000000}{10004}\approx 299.88
$$

which is large and positive, consistent with $s(x)\sim 3x\to+\infty$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Write the cubic dominated by its leading term:

$$
r(x)=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d
$$

$$
r(x)=ax^{3}\Bigl(1+\frac{b}{ax}+\frac{c}{ax^{2}}+\frac{d}{ax^{3}}\Bigr)
$$

As $x\to-\infty$:

$$
x\to-\infty
$$

$$
x^{2}=(-|x|)^{2}=|x|^{2}\to+\infty
$$

$$
x^{3}=(-|x|)^{3}=-|x|^{3}\to-\infty
$$

With $a>0$:

$$
a>0
$$

$$
ax^{3}\to-\infty
$$

Each correction term vanishes:

$$
\frac{b}{ax}\to 0
$$

$$
\frac{c}{ax^{2}}\to 0
$$

$$
\frac{d}{ax^{3}}\to 0
$$

so the parenthesis tends to $1$ and

$$
\lim_{x\to-\infty}r(x)=-\infty
$$

Numerical check with $a=3$, $b=c=d=0$ at $x=-10$:

$$
(-10)^{3}=-1000
$$

$$
3\cdot(-1000)=-3000
$$

$$
r(-10)=-3000
$$

At $x=-100$:

$$
(-100)^{2}=10000
$$

$$
(-100)^{3}=-1000000
$$

$$
3\cdot(-1000000)=-3000000
$$

$$
r(-100)=-3000000
$$

$$
-3000000<-3000
$$

which grows more negative as $x\to-\infty$, consistent with the limit $-\infty$ whenever $a>0$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Differentiate the cubic coefficient by coefficient:

$$
r(x)=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d
$$

$$
\frac{d}{dx}(ax^{3})=3ax^{2}
$$

$$
\frac{d}{dx}(bx^{2})=2bx
$$

$$
\frac{d}{dx}(cx)=c
$$

$$
\frac{d}{dx}(d)=0
$$

$$
r'(x)=3ax^{2}+2bx+c
$$

The hypothesis gives two vanishing conditions at $x=2$:

$$
r(2)=0
$$

$$
r'(2)=0
$$

A standard factorisation fact: if a polynomial and its first derivative both vanish at $\alpha$, then $(x-\alpha)^{2}$ divides the polynomial. Taking $\alpha=2$:

$$
(x-2)^{2}\mid r(x)
$$

Hence $x=2$ is at least a double root.

Concrete illustration with $a=1$, $b=-4$, $c=4$, $d=0$ so $r(x)=x(x-2)^{2}$:

$$
r(x)=x(x^{2}-4x+4)
$$

$$
r(x)=x^{3}-4x^{2}+4x
$$

$$
r'(x)=3x^{2}-8x+4
$$

Evaluate at $x=2$:

$$
r(2)=8-16+8=0
$$

$$
r'(2)=12-16+4=0
$$

and the factor $(x-2)^{2}$ is visible by construction. The claimed implication holds.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

From the asymptotic rewrite:

$$
s(x)=ax\cdot\frac{1+\frac{b}{ax}+\frac{c}{ax^{2}}+\frac{d}{ax^{3}}}{1+\frac{4}{x^{2}}}
$$

$$
s(x)\sim ax
$$

Degree comparison:

$$
\deg r=3
$$

$$
\deg(x^{2}+4)=2
$$

$$
3-2=1
$$

$$
3>2
$$

Because $a\neq 0$:

$$
|a|>0
$$

$$
|ax|\to\infty\qquad\text{as }|x|\to\infty
$$

$$
|s(x)|\to\infty\qquad\text{as }|x|\to\infty
$$

A horizontal asymptote $y=0$ would require

$$
s(x)\to 0
$$

but that contradicts $|s(x)|\to\infty$.

Numerical counter-example with $a=3$, $b=c=d=0$:

$$
s(100)=\frac{3\cdot 100^{3}}{100^{2}+4}
$$

$$
100^{2}=10000
$$

$$
100^{3}=1000000
$$

$$
3\cdot 1000000=3000000
$$

$$
10000+4=10004
$$

$$
\frac{3000000}{10004}\approx 299.88
$$

$$
299.88\neq 0
$$

and the values grow without bound as $|x|$ grows. So $y=0$ is not a horizontal asymptote for any coefficients with $a\neq 0$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Substitute $a=3$, $b=-6$, $c=0$, $d=0$:

$$
r(x)=3x^{3}+(-6)x^{2}+0\cdot x+0
$$

$$
r(x)=3x^{3}-6x^{2}
$$

Factor out the common monomial $3x^{2}$:

$$
3x^{3}=3x^{2}\cdot x
$$

$$
-6x^{2}=3x^{2}\cdot(-2)
$$

$$
3x^{3}-6x^{2}=3x^{2}\bigl(x-2\bigr)
$$

$$
r(x)=3x^{2}(x-2)
$$

Expand to verify:

$$
3x^{2}\cdot x=3x^{3}
$$

$$
3x^{2}\cdot(-2)=-6x^{2}
$$

$$
3x^{3}+(-6x^{2})=3x^{3}-6x^{2}
$$

Roots from the factorisation: $x=0$ from $x^{2}$ (multiplicity $2$), and $x=2$ from $x-2$ (multiplicity $1$).

Confirm with the derivative test at $x=0$:

$$
r'(x)=9x^{2}-12x
$$

$$
r'(0)=0
$$

$$
r(0)=0
$$

so multiplicity at least $2$ at $0$. At $x=2$:

$$
r(2)=3\cdot 4\cdot 0=0
$$

$$
r'(2)=9\cdot 4-12\cdot 2
$$

$$
9\cdot 4=36
$$

$$
12\cdot 2=24
$$

$$
36-24=12
$$

$$
r'(2)=12\neq 0
$$

so $x=2$ is a simple root. The claim holds.

So the statement is True.

math.title: Entangled exponential–log pair — hard compare
math.context:
Define the entangled pair
$$
f(t)=4e^{0.3t},\qquad g(t)=16e^{-0.6t}\qquad(t\in\mathbb{R}),
$$
and the log-gap
$$
h(t)=\ln f(t)-\ln g(t)=\ln\!\bigl(f(t)/g(t)\bigr).
$$
Also write $p(t)=f(t)\,g(t)$. Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: $f(t)=g(t)$ has the unique real solution $t=\dfrac{1}{0.9}\ln 4=\dfrac{\ln 4}{0.9}$.
$h(t)=\ln 4+0.9t$ for every real $t$, so $h$ is affine with positive slope $0.9$.
If $t$ increases by $\dfrac{10}{3}$, then $f$ is multiplied by $e$ and $g$ is multiplied by $e^{-2}$.
The product $p(t)=f(t)g(t)$ is minimized over $\mathbb{R}$ at the same $t$ where $f=g$, and that minimum value equals $64$.
Because $f(0)=4<16=g(0)$ and $f$ grows while $g$ decays, one has $f(t)<g(t)$ for every $t>0$.
math.solution_overview:
Two exponential trajectories and the log-gap between them. Every letter follows from the closed forms derived below.

**Part 1: Setup.**

$$
f(t)=4e^{0.3t}
$$

$$
g(t)=16e^{-0.6t}
$$

$$
h(t)=\ln\bigl(f(t)/g(t)\bigr)
$$

$$
p(t)=f(t)\,g(t)
$$

**Part 2: Ratio, log-gap, and product — every factor.**

Form the ratio:

$$
\frac{f(t)}{g(t)}=\frac{4e^{0.3t}}{16e^{-0.6t}}
$$

Constant prefactor:

$$
\frac{4}{16}=\frac{1}{4}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{4}=0.25
$$

Exponential exponent:

$$
0.3t-(-0.6t)=0.3t+0.6t
$$

$$
0.3+0.6=0.9
$$

$$
\frac{f(t)}{g(t)}=\frac{1}{4}e^{0.9t}
$$

Log-gap:

$$
h(t)=\ln\Bigl(\frac{1}{4}e^{0.9t}\Bigr)
$$

$$
\ln\Bigl(\frac{1}{4}\Bigr)+\ln(e^{0.9t})
$$

$$
\ln\Bigl(\frac{1}{4}\Bigr)=-\ln 4
$$

$$
\ln 4=\ln(2^{2})=2\ln 2
$$

$$
\ln 2\approx 0.693147
$$

$$
2\times 0.693147=1.386294
$$

$$
\ln 4\approx 1.386294
$$

$$
\ln(e^{0.9t})=0.9t
$$

$$
h(t)=-\ln 4+0.9t
$$

Product:

$$
p(t)=4e^{0.3t}\cdot 16e^{-0.6t}
$$

$$
4\times 16=64
$$

$$
0.3t+(-0.6t)=-0.3t
$$

$$
p(t)=64e^{-0.3t}
$$

**Part 3: Crossing point.**

Set $f=g$:

$$
4e^{0.3t}=16e^{-0.6t}
$$

$$
\frac{4}{16}e^{0.9t}=1
$$

$$
\frac{1}{4}e^{0.9t}=1
$$

$$
e^{0.9t}=4
$$

$$
0.9t=\ln 4
$$

$$
t=\frac{\ln 4}{0.9}
$$

$$
\frac{1.386294}{0.9}\approx 1.540327
$$
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Set the two trajectories equal:

$$
4e^{0.3t}=16e^{-0.6t}
$$

Divide both sides by $4$:

$$
e^{0.3t}=4e^{-0.6t}
$$

Multiply both sides by $e^{0.6t}$:

$$
e^{0.3t}e^{0.6t}=4
$$

$$
0.3+0.6=0.9
$$

$$
e^{0.9t}=4
$$

Take the natural log:

$$
0.9t=\ln 4
$$

$$
t=\frac{\ln 4}{0.9}
$$

Equivalently:

$$
t=\frac{1}{0.9}\ln 4
$$

Build $\ln 4$ numerically for a cross-check:

$$
\ln 2\approx 0.693147
$$

$$
\ln 4=2\ln 2
$$

$$
2\times 0.693147=1.386294
$$

$$
\frac{1.386294}{0.9}
$$

$$
\frac{1.386294}{0.9}=1.5403266\ldots
$$

$$
t^{*}\approx 1.540327
$$

Uniqueness: the map $t\mapsto e^{0.9t}$ is strictly increasing (derivative $0.9e^{0.9t}>0$), hence one-to-one on $\mathbb{R}$. Verify $f(t^{*})=g(t^{*})$ via the ratio:

$$
\frac{f(t^{*})}{g(t^{*})}=\frac{1}{4}e^{0.9t^{*}}
$$

$$
e^{0.9t^{*}}=e^{\ln 4}=4
$$

$$
\frac{1}{4}\times 4=1
$$

so $f(t^{*})=g(t^{*})$ holds.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Expand the log-gap from first principles:

$$
h(t)=\ln f(t)-\ln g(t)
$$

$$
h(t)=\ln\Bigl(\frac{4e^{0.3t}}{16e^{-0.6t}}\Bigr)
$$

Prefactor:

$$
\frac{4}{16}=\frac{1}{4}
$$

Exponent:

$$
0.3-(-0.6)=0.9
$$

$$
\frac{f(t)}{g(t)}=\frac{1}{4}e^{0.9t}
$$

$$
h(t)=\ln\Bigl(\frac{1}{4}e^{0.9t}\Bigr)
$$

$$
h(t)=\ln\Bigl(\frac{1}{4}\Bigr)+0.9t
$$

$$
\ln\Bigl(\frac{1}{4}\Bigr)=-\ln 4
$$

$$
h(t)=-\ln 4+0.9t
$$

The claim writes $\ln 4+0.9t$. Compare constant terms:

$$
\ln 4\approx 1.386294
$$

$$
-\ln 4\approx -1.386294
$$

$$
-\ln 4\neq\ln 4
$$

Evaluate both formulas at $t=0$:

$$
h(0)=\ln\Bigl(\frac{4}{16}\Bigr)=\ln\Bigl(\frac{1}{4}\Bigr)
$$

$$
\ln\Bigl(\frac{1}{4}\Bigr)=-\ln 4\approx -1.386294
$$

Claimed value at $t=0$:

$$
\ln 4+0.9\cdot 0=\ln 4\approx 1.386294
$$

$$
-1.386294\neq 1.386294
$$

The slope $0.9$ is correct, but the claimed constant $+\ln 4$ has the wrong sign.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Shift the argument of $f$ by $\dfrac{10}{3}$:

$$
f\Bigl(t+\frac{10}{3}\Bigr)=4\exp\Bigl(0.3\Bigl(t+\frac{10}{3}\Bigr)\Bigr)
$$

Compute the extra piece of the exponent:

$$
0.3\cdot\frac{10}{3}
$$

$$
0.3\times 10=3
$$

$$
\frac{3}{3}=1
$$

$$
0.3\cdot\frac{10}{3}=1
$$

$$
f\Bigl(t+\frac{10}{3}\Bigr)=4e^{0.3t+1}
$$

$$
4e^{0.3t+1}=e\cdot\bigl(4e^{0.3t}\bigr)
$$

$$
f\Bigl(t+\frac{10}{3}\Bigr)=e\cdot f(t)
$$

Shift $g$ by the same amount:

$$
g\Bigl(t+\frac{10}{3}\Bigr)=16\exp\Bigl(-0.6\Bigl(t+\frac{10}{3}\Bigr)\Bigr)
$$

Extra piece of the exponent:

$$
-0.6\cdot\frac{10}{3}
$$

$$
0.6\times 10=6
$$

$$
\frac{6}{3}=2
$$

$$
-0.6\cdot\frac{10}{3}=-2
$$

$$
g\Bigl(t+\frac{10}{3}\Bigr)=16e^{-0.6t-2}
$$

$$
16e^{-0.6t-2}=e^{-2}\cdot\bigl(16e^{-0.6t}\bigr)
$$

$$
g\Bigl(t+\frac{10}{3}\Bigr)=e^{-2}g(t)
$$

Cross-check the shift size:

$$
\frac{10}{3}\approx 3.333333
$$

$$
0.3\times 3.333333\approx 1.000000
$$

$$
-0.6\times 3.333333\approx -2.000000
$$

So $f$ is multiplied by $e$ and $g$ is multiplied by $e^{-2}$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Form the product explicitly:

$$
p(t)=4e^{0.3t}\cdot 16e^{-0.6t}
$$

Constant factor:

$$
4\times 16=64
$$

Exponent sum:

$$
0.3t+(-0.6t)=-0.3t
$$

$$
p(t)=64e^{-0.3t}
$$

Derivative of the product:

$$
p'(t)=64\cdot(-0.3)e^{-0.3t}
$$

$$
-0.3\times 64=-19.2
$$

$$
p'(t)=-19.2\,e^{-0.3t}
$$

Since $e^{-0.3t}>0$ for all real $t$:

$$
p'(t)<0
$$

for every $t$, so $p$ is strictly decreasing on $\mathbb{R}$ and has no global minimiser.

At the crossing $t^{*}=\dfrac{\ln 4}{0.9}$:

$$
\ln 4\approx 1.386294
$$

$$
t^{*}\approx\frac{1.386294}{0.9}\approx 1.540327
$$

$$
p(t^{*})=64e^{-0.3\cdot t^{*}}
$$

$$
0.3\times 1.540327=0.462098
$$

$$
\frac{0.3}{0.9}=\frac{1}{3}
$$

$$
0.3\cdot\frac{\ln 4}{0.9}=\frac{\ln 4}{3}
$$

$$
e^{-(\ln 4)/3}=4^{-1/3}
$$

$$
4^{1/3}\approx 1.587401
$$

$$
4^{-1/3}\approx 0.629961
$$

$$
64\times 0.629961\approx 40.3175
$$

$$
p(t^{*})\approx 40.3175
$$

Compare with the claimed minimum value $64$:

$$
40.3175\neq 64
$$

Both halves of the claim fail: there is no minimum at the crossing, and the product value there is not $64$.

So the statement is False.

math.title: Tangled revenue path — marginal analysis
math.context: A firm faces inverse demand $P(q)=90-3q$ for $0\le q\le 30$ (price in euros, quantity in thousands of units). Revenue is $R(q)=q\cdot P(q)$. Marginal revenue means $R'(q)$. Decide whether each claim is true or false.
statements: $R'(q)=90-6q$, so in particular $R'(4)=66$.
Revenue is maximised at the same quantity where $P(q)=0$, i.e. at the choke quantity $q=30$.
If output rises from $q=4$ to $q=5$, the linear approximation using $R'(4)$ overestimates the true revenue increase $R(5)-R(4)$, because $R$ is a concave quadratic.
At the quantity that maximises $R$, price equals marginal revenue.
Cutting price enough to raise quantity from $q=16$ to $q=17$ must raise revenue, because more units are sold.
math.solution_overview:
Linear inverse demand produces a concave quadratic revenue path. Marginal revenue is the derivative; the revenue peak is where that derivative vanishes.

**Part 1: Setup.**

$$
P(q)=90-3q,\qquad 0\le q\le 30
$$

$$
R(q)=q\cdot P(q)
$$

$$
R(q)=q(90-3q)
$$

$$
q\cdot 90=90q
$$

$$
q\cdot(-3q)=-3q^{2}
$$

$$
R(q)=90q-3q^{2}
$$

**Part 2: Marginal revenue and the peak.**

Differentiate term by term:

$$
\frac{d}{dq}(90q)=90
$$

$$
\frac{d}{dq}(-3q^{2})=-6q
$$

$$
R'(q)=90-6q
$$

Second derivative:

$$
R''(q)=-6
$$

$$
-6<0
$$

so $R$ is strictly concave. Set marginal revenue to zero:

$$
90-6q=0
$$

$$
6q=90
$$

$$
q=\frac{90}{6}
$$

$$
\frac{90}{6}=15
$$

$$
q^{*}=15
$$

**Part 3: Values at key quantities.**

At the peak $q=15$:

$$
3\times 15=45
$$

$$
P(15)=90-45=45
$$

$$
6\times 15=90
$$

$$
R'(15)=90-90=0
$$

$$
15^{2}=225
$$

$$
90\times 15=1350
$$

$$
3\times 225=675
$$

$$
R(15)=1350-675=675
$$

At the choke quantity $q=30$:

$$
3\times 30=90
$$

$$
P(30)=90-90=0
$$

$$
R(30)=30\times 0=0
$$

At $q=4$ and $q=5$ (used in letter C):

$$
R(4)=360-48=312
$$

$$
R(5)=450-75=375
$$

$$
R(5)-R(4)=63
$$

$$
R'(4)=66
$$
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Expand revenue from inverse demand:

$$
P(q)=90-3q
$$

$$
R(q)=q\cdot P(q)
$$

$$
R(q)=q(90-3q)
$$

Distribute:

$$
q\cdot 90=90q
$$

$$
q\cdot(-3q)=-3q^{2}
$$

$$
R(q)=90q-3q^{2}
$$

Differentiate the first term:

$$
\frac{d}{dq}(90q)=90
$$

Differentiate the second term:

$$
\frac{d}{dq}(-3q^{2})=-3\cdot 2q
$$

$$
3\cdot 2=6
$$

$$
-3\cdot 2=-6
$$

$$
-3\cdot 2q=-6q
$$

$$
R'(q)=90-6q
$$

Evaluate at $q=4$:

$$
6\times 4=24
$$

$$
90-24
$$

$$
90-20=70
$$

$$
70-4=66
$$

$$
90-24=66
$$

$$
R'(4)=66
$$

Cross-check by evaluating $R(4)$ fully:

$$
90\times 4=360
$$

$$
4^{2}=16
$$

$$
3\times 16=48
$$

$$
360-48
$$

$$
360-50=310
$$

$$
310+2=312
$$

$$
R(4)=312
$$

Also check $R'(5)$ for consistency of the formula:

$$
6\times 5=30
$$

$$
90-30=60
$$

$$
R'(5)=60
$$

The claimed formula $R'(q)=90-6q$ and the particular value $R'(4)=66$ both hold.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Maximise $R$ by setting marginal revenue to zero:

$$
R'(q)=90-6q
$$

$$
90-6q=0
$$

$$
6q=90
$$

$$
q=\frac{90}{6}
$$

$$
\frac{90}{6}=15
$$

$$
q^{*}=15
$$

Confirm it is a maximum via the second derivative:

$$
R''(q)=-6
$$

$$
-6<0
$$

Choke price $P(q)=0$ forces:

$$
90-3q=0
$$

$$
3q=90
$$

$$
q=\frac{90}{3}
$$

$$
\frac{90}{3}=30
$$

$$
q_{\mathrm{choke}}=30
$$

Compare the two quantities:

$$
15\neq 30
$$

$$
30-15=15
$$

Revenue at the peak:

$$
90\times 15
$$

$$
90\times 10=900
$$

$$
90\times 5=450
$$

$$
900+450=1350
$$

$$
15^{2}=225
$$

$$
3\times 225
$$

$$
3\times 200=600
$$

$$
3\times 25=75
$$

$$
600+75=675
$$

$$
1350-675=675
$$

$$
R(15)=675
$$

Revenue at the choke:

$$
3\times 30=90
$$

$$
P(30)=90-90=0
$$

$$
R(30)=30\times 0=0
$$

$$
675\neq 0
$$

Revenue is maximised at $q=15$, not at the choke quantity $q=30$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Compute $R(4)$ in pieces:

$$
90\times 4=360
$$

$$
4^{2}=16
$$

$$
3\times 16=48
$$

$$
360-48
$$

$$
360-40=320
$$

$$
320-8=312
$$

$$
R(4)=312
$$

Compute $R(5)$ in pieces:

$$
90\times 5=450
$$

$$
5^{2}=25
$$

$$
3\times 25=75
$$

$$
450-75
$$

$$
450-70=380
$$

$$
380-5=375
$$

$$
R(5)=375
$$

True increment:

$$
R(5)-R(4)=375-312
$$

$$
375-300=75
$$

$$
75-12=63
$$

$$
375-312=63
$$

Linear approximation using $R'(4)$:

$$
6\times 4=24
$$

$$
90-24=66
$$

$$
R'(4)=66
$$

Step size:

$$
5-4=1
$$

$$
R'(4)\cdot 1=66\times 1
$$

$$
66\times 1=66
$$

Compare approximation to truth:

$$
66-63=3
$$

$$
66>63
$$

Confirm concavity:

$$
R''(q)=-6
$$

$$
-6<0
$$

Because $R$ is a concave quadratic, the tangent overestimates the true increment by EUR $3$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The revenue-maximising quantity solves $R'(q)=0$:

$$
R'(q)=90-6q
$$

$$
90-6q=0
$$

$$
6q=90
$$

$$
q=\frac{90}{6}
$$

$$
\frac{90}{6}=15
$$

$$
q^{*}=15
$$

Marginal revenue at that point:

$$
6\times 15=90
$$

$$
90-90=0
$$

$$
R'(15)=0
$$

Price at the same quantity:

$$
3\times 15=45
$$

$$
90-45=45
$$

$$
P(15)=45
$$

Compare price and marginal revenue:

$$
45\neq 0
$$

$$
P(15)-R'(15)=45-0
$$

$$
45-0=45
$$

$$
P(15)\neq R'(15)
$$

Also record revenue there for context:

$$
90\times 15
$$

$$
90\times 10=900
$$

$$
90\times 5=450
$$

$$
900+450=1350
$$

$$
15^{2}=225
$$

$$
3\times 225=675
$$

$$
1350-675=675
$$

$$
R(15)=675
$$

Price would equal marginal revenue only if $90-3q=90-6q$, which forces $3q=0$ hence $q=0$, not the peak. At the revenue peak, price is EUR $45$ while marginal revenue is $0$.

So the statement is False.

math.title: A Positive Test in a Deer Population
math.context: In a wild deer population, 60% are Subspecies A, 25% are Subspecies B, and 15% are Subspecies C. A certain prion disease is present in 2% of Subspecies A, 6% of Subspecies B, and 15% of Subspecies C. A field test for the disease has a 90% sensitivity (probability of a positive result if the deer truly has the disease) and a 4% false-positive rate (probability of a positive result if the deer does not have the disease), regardless of subspecies. A randomly tested deer receives a POSITIVE result.
statements: The probability that a tested deer receives a positive result is greater than 7%.
The probability that the deer is Subspecies A AND receives a positive result is greater than 3.4%.
The probability that the deer is Subspecies A, given a positive result is greater than 45%.
The probability that a tested deer receives a negative result equals 1 minus the probability that a tested deer receives a positive result.
The probability that the deer is Subspecies C, given a positive result is greater than the probability that the deer is Subspecies B, given a positive result.
tactical_explanations:
**D.** → True

A field test returns either a positive or a negative result. Those two outcomes partition the sample space:

$$
T^{-}=(T^{+})^{c}
$$

$$
T^{+}\cup T^{-}=\Omega
$$

$$
T^{+}\cap T^{-}=\emptyset
$$

Probability of a complement is one minus the probability of the event:

$$
P(T^{-})=1-P(T^{+})
$$

Rebuild $P(T^{+})$ so the identity is numerical as well:

$$
0.90\times 0.02=0.018
$$

$$
0.04\times 0.98=0.0392
$$

$$
0.018+0.0392=0.0572
$$

$$
0.0572\times 0.60=0.03432
$$

$$
0.90\times 0.06=0.054
$$

$$
0.04\times 0.94=0.0376
$$

$$
0.054+0.0376=0.0916
$$

$$
0.0916\times 0.25=0.0229
$$

$$
0.90\times 0.15=0.135
$$

$$
0.04\times 0.85=0.034
$$

$$
0.135+0.034=0.169
$$

$$
0.169\times 0.15=0.02535
$$

$$
0.03432+0.0229=0.05722
$$

$$
0.05722+0.02535=0.08257
$$

$$
P(T^{+})=0.08257
$$

$$
1-0.08257=0.91743
$$

$$
P(T^{-})=0.91743
$$

The equality $P(T^{-})=1-P(T^{+})$ holds by complementarity alone — no prevalence assumption is required. The claim asserts exactly that identity.

So the statement is True.
math.solution_overview:
A randomly tested deer from a three-subspecies population returns a positive field-test result. Every letter reuses the subspecies-conditional positive rates and the law-of-total-probability marginal derived below.

**Part 1: Priors and prevalences.**

$$
P(S_A)=0.60
$$

$$
P(S_B)=0.25
$$

$$
P(S_C)=0.15
$$

$$
P(D\mid S_A)=0.02
$$

$$
P(D\mid S_B)=0.06
$$

$$
P(D\mid S_C)=0.15
$$

Disease-free complements:

$$
1-0.02=0.98
$$

$$
P(D^{c}\mid S_A)=0.98
$$

$$
1-0.06=0.94
$$

$$
P(D^{c}\mid S_B)=0.94
$$

$$
1-0.15=0.85
$$

$$
P(D^{c}\mid S_C)=0.85
$$

Test characteristics:

$$
P(T^{+}\mid D)=0.90
$$

$$
P(T^{+}\mid D^{c})=0.04
$$

**Part 2: Subspecies-conditional positive rates — every product.**

$$
P(T^{+}\mid S_i)=0.90\cdot P(D\mid S_i)+0.04\cdot P(D^{c}\mid S_i)
$$

Subspecies A:

$$
0.90\times 0.02=0.018
$$

$$
0.04\times 0.98=0.0392
$$

$$
0.018+0.0392=0.0572
$$

$$
P(T^{+}\mid S_A)=0.0572
$$

Subspecies B:

$$
0.90\times 0.06=0.054
$$

$$
0.04\times 0.94=0.0376
$$

$$
0.054+0.0376=0.0916
$$

$$
P(T^{+}\mid S_B)=0.0916
$$

Subspecies C:

$$
0.90\times 0.15=0.135
$$

$$
0.04\times 0.85=0.034
$$

$$
0.135+0.034=0.169
$$

$$
P(T^{+}\mid S_C)=0.169
$$

**Part 3: Marginal $P(T^{+})$ and joints.**

$$
0.0572\times 0.60=0.03432
$$

$$
0.0916\times 0.25=0.0229
$$

$$
0.169\times 0.15=0.02535
$$

$$
0.03432+0.0229=0.05722
$$

$$
0.05722+0.02535=0.08257
$$

$$
P(T^{+})=0.08257
$$

$$
P(S_A\cap T^{+})=0.03432
$$

$$
P(S_B\cap T^{+})=0.0229
$$

$$
P(S_C\cap T^{+})=0.02535
$$

$$
P(S_A\mid T^{+})=\frac{0.03432}{0.08257}\approx 0.4156
$$

$$
P(S_B\mid T^{+})=\frac{0.0229}{0.08257}\approx 0.2773
$$

$$
P(S_C\mid T^{+})=\frac{0.02535}{0.08257}\approx 0.3070
$$

math.title: Harbor Foghorn Tests
math.context: Harbor staff run 14 independent foghorn tests. The expected number of clear audible tests is 11.2. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The next test fails with probability 0.2.
The expected number of audible tests in the next 12 tests is 4.8.
The variance of the number of audible tests out of 50 tests is 8.
The probability of 3 consecutive audible tests is less than 0.3.
The probability of at most 4 audible tests in the next 6 tests is more than 0.5.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

From the stem quantities, recover the common success probability:

$$
E[X]=np
$$

$$
n=14
$$

$$
E[X]=11.2
$$

$$
p=\frac{11.2}{14}
$$

Check by multiplication, splitting $14\times 0.8$:

$$
14\times 0.8
$$

$$
10\times 0.8=8
$$

$$
4\times 0.8=3.2
$$

$$
8+3.2=11.2
$$

$$
14\times 0.8=11.2
$$

$$
\frac{11.2}{14}=0.8
$$

$$
p=0.8
$$

Each independent trial either succeeds or fails, so the failure probability is the complement:

$$
1-p
$$

$$
1-0.8
$$

$$
1.0-0.8=0.2
$$

$$
1-p=0.2
$$

The next test fails with probability $0.2$, matching the claim. Cross-check: expected failures in the original block of $14$:

$$
14\times 0.2
$$

$$
10\times 0.2=2
$$

$$
4\times 0.2=0.8
$$

$$
2+0.8=2.8
$$

$$
14\times 0.2=2.8
$$

$$
14-11.2
$$

$$
14-11=3
$$

$$
3-0.2=2.8
$$

$$
14-11.2=2.8
$$

$$
2.8=2.8
$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

For a binomial count $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, the mean is

$$
E[X]=np
$$

Recover $p$ again from the stem:

$$
E[X]=11.2
$$

$$
n=14
$$

$$
p=\frac{11.2}{14}
$$

$$
14\times 0.8=11.2
$$

$$
p=0.8
$$

$$
1-p=0.2
$$

Use the new trial count $n=12$:

$$
E[X]=12\times 0.8
$$

Split the product:

$$
12\times 0.8
$$

$$
10\times 0.8=8
$$

$$
2\times 0.8=1.6
$$

$$
8+1.6=9.6
$$

$$
E[X]=9.6
$$

The claim reports $4.8$. Compare:

$$
9.6\neq 4.8
$$

$$
9.6-4.8=4.8
$$

Note that $4.8$ would equal $12\times 0.4$:

$$
12\times 0.4
$$

$$
10\times 0.4=4
$$

$$
2\times 0.4=0.8
$$

$$
4+0.8=4.8
$$

$$
12\times 0.4=4.8
$$

which uses the wrong success probability $0.4$ instead of the recovered $p=0.8$. The correct expectation for the next $12$ tests is $9.6$, not $4.8$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

For $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, the variance formula is

$$
\mathrm{Var}(X)=np(1-p)
$$

Recover $p$ from the stem:

$$
p=\frac{11.2}{14}
$$

$$
14\times 0.8=11.2
$$

$$
p=0.8
$$

$$
1-p=1-0.8
$$

$$
1-0.8=0.2
$$

$$
1-p=0.2
$$

Insert $n=50$:

$$
\mathrm{Var}(X)=50\times 0.8\times 0.2
$$

First product $50\times 0.8$:

$$
50\times 0.8
$$

$$
50\times \frac{4}{5}
$$

$$
\frac{50\times 4}{5}=\frac{200}{5}=40
$$

$$
50\times 0.8=40
$$

Second product $40\times 0.2$:

$$
40\times 0.2
$$

$$
40\times 0.2=8
$$

$$
\mathrm{Var}(X)=8
$$

Alternatively group as $50\times(0.8\times 0.2)$:

$$
0.8\times 0.2=0.16
$$

$$
50\times 0.16
$$

$$
50\times 0.10=5
$$

$$
50\times 0.06=3
$$

$$
5+3=8
$$

$$
50\times 0.16=8
$$

Same result either way. The variance stated in the claim matches.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Independence across trials means a run of successes multiplies the same probability $p$ on every trial:

$$
P(\text{3 consecutive audible})=p\cdot p\cdot p
$$

$$
p\cdot p\cdot p=p^{3}
$$

Recover $p$:

$$
p=\frac{11.2}{14}
$$

$$
14\times 0.8=11.2
$$

$$
p=0.8
$$

$$
p^{3}=(0.8)^{3}
$$

Build the power one multiplication at a time:

$$
0.8\times 0.8=0.64
$$

$$
(0.8)^{2}=0.64
$$

$$
0.64\times 0.8
$$

$$
0.64\times 0.8=0.512
$$

$$
(0.8)^{3}=0.512
$$

Compare with the claimed cutoff $0.3$:

$$
0.512-0.3=0.212
$$

$$
0.512>0.3
$$

As a percentage check:

$$
0.512=51.2\%
$$

$$
0.3=30\%
$$

$$
51.2\%>30\%
$$

Also note $(0.8)^{3}=0.512$ is more than half, while $0.3$ is less than one third. The probability is greater than $0.3$, not less. The claim's inequality fails.

So the statement is False.
math.solution_overview:
Harbor staff run independent foghorn tests whose clear-audible outcomes form a binomial count. The stem supplies the mean over a block of $14$ trials; every letter reuses the recovered success probability $p=0.8$.

**Part 1: Setup.**

$$
X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)
$$

Stem data:

$$
n=14
$$

$$
E[X]=11.2
$$

Mean and variance identities:

$$
E[X]=np
$$

$$
\mathrm{Var}(X)=np(1-p)
$$

**Part 2: Recover $p$ by division.**

$$
p=\frac{E[X]}{n}=\frac{11.2}{14}
$$

$$
14\times 0.8=11.2
$$

$$
\frac{11.2}{14}=0.8
$$

$$
p=0.8
$$

$$
1-p=1-0.8
$$

$$
1-0.8=0.2
$$

$$
1-p=0.2
$$

**Part 3: Shared downstream values.**

Expected audible count in $12$ trials:

$$
12\times 0.8=9.6
$$

Variance in $50$ trials:

$$
50\times 0.8=40
$$

$$
40\times 0.2=8
$$

Three consecutive successes — build the cube:

$$
0.8\times 0.8=0.64
$$

$$
0.64\times 0.8=0.512
$$

$$
(0.8)^{3}=0.512
$$

Lower tail for $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(6,0.8)$:

$$
P(X\le 4)=\sum_{x=0}^{4}\binom{6}{x}(0.8)^{x}(0.2)^{6-x}=0.34464
$$

which is less than $0.5$ (full expansion in letter E).
